conclusion.label: rejects

report:
### Conclusion
Contrary to your initial assumption, high-quality medical evidence indicates that arthroscopic surgery (joint endoscopy) does **not** provide meaningful, long-term benefits for knee osteoarthritis compared to non-surgical care or placebo procedures.

### Evidence
* **Landmark Placebo-Controlled Trials:** A pivotal randomized controlled trial evaluated arthroscopic joint lavage and debridement against a placebo (sham) surgery in patients with knee osteoarthritis. The study revealed that patient outcomes regarding pain and joint function were no better after arthroscopy than after the placebo procedure (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259).
* **Medical Practice Guidelines:** Major clinical guidelines advise against performing arthroscopy for degenerative knee conditions:
  * The **American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS)** explicitly recommends against arthroscopic debridement or lavage for primary knee osteoarthritis, noting no significant advantage over non-operative treatments (https://scispace.com/papers/a-review-of-2021-and-2022-aaos-guidelines-for-meniscal-50ox5zjpmc, https://www.aetna.com/cpb/medical/data/600_699/0673.html).
  * Expert panel recommendations published in the **BMJ** strongly advise against arthroscopic surgery for degenerative knee disease, based on evidence showing it fails to produce meaningful improvements in pain or function compared to conservative management such as exercise therapy (https://bjsm.bmj.com/content/52/5/313).

Overall, robust scientific evidence demonstrates that arthroscopy is generally ineffective as a routine treatment for knee osteoarthritis.
